subject: General Aptitude
summary: grammar, vocabulary, sentence completion, analogies, para-jumbles and reading comprehension
next_day: Strength of Materials, Deflection of Beams

questions.text: Select the correct option to fill the blank: The quality of the castings ______ improved since the new furnace was installed.
solution: Concept: The verb agrees with the head noun of the subject, not with the noun inside the 'of' phrase.
Head noun: quality (singular) → 'has improved'. 'Castings' is only the object of 'of'.
'Since …' needs the present perfect, which also rules out 'were'.
Exam tip: Strike out the 'of …' phrase and read the sentence again: 'The quality has improved'.

questions.text: Select the word closest in meaning to PRAGMATIC.
solution: Concept: Pragmatic = dealing with things sensibly and realistically.
Closest: practical. 'Idealistic' is nearly the opposite; 'dogmatic' and 'talkative' are sound or look-alike traps.
Exam tip: In GATE synonym questions, eliminate words with the opposite tone first.

questions.text: Select the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to OBSCURE (as an adjective).
solution: Concept: Obscure = not clear, hard to understand or little known.
Opposite: evident (plain, clearly seen). 'Vague' and 'hidden' are near-synonyms; 'remote' is unrelated.
Exam tip: Check the part of speech: 'obscure' is also a verb (to hide), but the antonym must match the adjective sense asked.
Concept: Instrument : quantity it measures.
An ammeter measures current; a tachometer measures rotational speed (rpm).
Torque: dynamometer; temperature: thermometer/pyrometer; pressure: manometer/Bourdon gauge.
Exam tip: State the relation in a sentence first, then test each option in the same sentence.

questions.text: How many of the following words are spelt correctly? necessary, recieve, occasion, accomodation, rhythm, privilege, maintainance
solution: Concept: Check each word letter by letter against the standard spelling.
Correct: necessary, occasion, rhythm, privilege → 4.
Wrong: receive, accommodation, maintenance.
Exam tip: 'i before e except after c' fixes receive; double letters (accommodation, embarrass) are frequent traps.

questions.text: Select the correct option to fill the blank: He is very good ______ solving numerical problems.
solution: Concept: Fixed preposition: good at (a skill or activity).
'Good in' is used for a subject in some regions but 'good at + -ing' is the standard form.
Exam tip: Learn adjective–preposition pairs: good at, interested in, capable of, responsible for.

questions.text: The idiom 'a blessing in disguise' means
opts: something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good
questions.ans: (A) something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good
solution: Meaning: an apparent misfortune that later proves helpful.
Example: Missing the bus was a blessing in disguise; I met the recruiter at the station.
Exam tip: Idiom questions in GATE GA are usually common ones; read them literally only to discard options.

questions.text: Arrange the sentences to form a coherent paragraph and enter the order as a four-digit number. (1) Sensors on the shaft now report vibration levels every second. (2) In the past, a pump was repaired only after it broke down. (3) When the readings drift from normal, a technician is sent before failure occurs. (4) This shift from reactive to predictive maintenance has cut unplanned stoppages sharply.
solution: Concept: Find the opening (no pronoun or connector pointing back), then follow the links.
2 sets the past situation ('In the past'); 1 the change ('now'); 3 uses 'the readings' from 1; 4 sums up with 'This shift'.
Order: 2134
Exam tip: Words like 'this', 'these', 'the readings', 'however' always point to an earlier sentence.

questions.text: Select the pair that best fills the blanks: Although the prototype was ______, the final product proved remarkably ______.
solution: Concept: 'Although' signals a contrast between the two blanks.
Only (A) gives opposite ideas: crude prototype, refined final product.
(B), (C) and (D) pair similar words, which do not fit 'although'.
Exam tip: Spot the connector first (although, because, and, but); it tells you same or opposite.

questions.text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (1) One of the valves / (2) were found / (3) to be leaking / (4) during the inspection.
solution: Concept: 'One of the + plural noun' takes a singular verb.
Subject: 'one' → 'was found'. The error is in part 2.
Exam tip: Compare with 'one of those who …', where the verb after 'who' is plural.

questions.text:
Passage: “Kaizen, the Japanese practice of continuous improvement, rests on a simple idea: large gains can come from many small changes. A worker who moves a tool rack closer to a machine saves a few seconds per cycle; across thousands of cycles and hundreds of workers, the saving becomes large. Critics point out that small steps cannot replace bold redesign when a process is fundamentally flawed. Supporters reply that the two are complementary: kaizen keeps a good process improving between the rare occasions when a radical change is justified.”
Which of the following is supported by the passage?
opts: Kaizen and occasional radical redesign can work together.
Small changes can never produce large gains.
Critics believe kaizen saves no time at all.
questions.ans: (A) Kaizen and occasional radical redesign can work together.
solution: Concept: Choose the option that the passage states or directly implies; reject extreme words (never, unnecessary).
The supporters' reply: 'the two are complementary' → (A).
(B) contradicts 'rare occasions when a radical change is justified'; (C) contradicts the main idea; (D) misstates the critics, who only say small steps cannot fix a flawed process.
Exam tip: In GATE RC, the right option is usually a paraphrase, not a copy, of one line.

questions.text:
Passage: “Kaizen, the Japanese practice of continuous improvement, rests on a simple idea: large gains can come from many small changes. A worker who moves a tool rack closer to a machine saves a few seconds per cycle; across thousands of cycles and hundreds of workers, the saving becomes large. Critics point out that small steps cannot replace bold redesign when a process is fundamentally flawed. Supporters reply that the two are complementary: kaizen keeps a good process improving between the rare occasions when a radical change is justified.”
The example of the tool rack is used mainly to
opts: show how small savings add up to a large gain
prove that critics of kaizen are wrong
questions.ans: (A) show how small savings add up to a large gain
solution: Concept: Ask why the author included the example.
A few seconds per cycle × thousands of cycles × hundreds of workers = large saving: it illustrates the 'many small changes' idea.
Exam tip: 'The example is used to …' questions are answered by the sentence just before the example.

questions.text: How many of the following sentences are grammatically correct? (i) Each of the boys has his own locker. (ii) I look forward to meet you. (iii) Neither of the answers is correct. (iv) He did not knew the answer. (v) The committee has submitted its report.
solution: Concept: Check agreement and verb forms in each sentence.
(i) correct: 'each' takes 'has'. (iii) correct: 'neither of' takes a singular verb. (v) correct: the committee acting as one body takes 'has … its'.
(ii) wrong: 'look forward to meeting' ('to' is a preposition here). (iv) wrong: 'did not know'.
Answer: 3
Exam tip: After did/does/do, the verb is always in its base form.

questions.text: Select the most appropriate word to fill the blank: The new storage dams will help ______ the effects of the drought.
solution: Concept: Confusable words.
Mitigate = make less severe (fits). Militate (against) = be a strong factor against; migrate = move; mediate = act as a go-between.
Exam tip: GATE loves look-alike pairs: mitigate/militate, affect/effect, complement/compliment, principal/principle.

questions.text: Which is the odd one out? Enter its number. (1) Anemometer (2) Barometer (3) Hygrometer (4) Stethoscope
solution: Concept: Find the common group.
Anemometer (wind speed), barometer (air pressure) and hygrometer (humidity) are weather instruments.
The stethoscope is a medical instrument → 4.
Exam tip: When two groupings seem possible, pick the one that leaves exactly one item out.
